docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: RunningMate is a desktop application for storing and analyzing sport activities, built with Rust and Tauri. In the current version it can handle running, cycling and walking activities. This is - and will be for a while - work in progress, so expect some bugs and missing features. But I try my best and I really "eat my own dogfood". I am using this for my own runs and rides, so the motivation is high to keep it running and add new features regulary.

docs.title: Why RunningMate?
docs.text:
I run and ride for over 25 years, I was never a pro, I never wanted to be one, but I always wanted to know how I am doing. A little data obsessed so to say. I like my stats, my charts and maps, not to compare myself with others, but with myself.

Over the years I used a lot of different tools and devices, from a handwritten running dairy to Excel sheets, from Garmin Connect to Strava, from Runtastic to NikeRun, I used it all. Most of the services are great, but they all have their limitations and flaws. From incorrect data to missing features, from privacy concerns to data export limitations. Not to mention the pricing.

The social aspect of most of the available services is not my thing. Personally, I find some of the virtual communities rather toxic and not particularly motivating. On top of that, leaderboards are almost always flooded with absurd scores. Same for my own “personal bests” - data that might look impressive, but is far from reality.

So if you are a bit like me, and you even use(d) different devices like polar, garmin, suunto, wahoo, etc. you might find yourself in the situation that you either have to pay to get more than a very basic history list, or you end up with a lot of raw data files or even worse, the data is gone for good. That is the reason why I started this project. A collection of tools to store, analyze and visualize your very own activity data.

And with that, happy running, riding, or walking! (There might be more in the future)

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Download the latest release from GitHub and open the installer for your system (on macOS the .dmg). The app is not code-signed yet, so macOS asks for confirmation the first time you open it.

All data stays on your computer in the RunningData folder in your home directory: the database, the archived activity files and your photos and videos. Activities come in through Sync: TCX and GPX files, a watched folder (e.g. an iCloud export) or Garmin Connect, which also works in the other direction.

docs.title: What's in the app
docs.text:
• Dashboard: latest photos, the last four weeks, goals, the training week, volume and an activity feed.
  • Activities: lists per sport with search, filters and a panel with the key figures.
  • Detail view: maps, charts, splits, zones, training effect, an AI summary, a social-share image and editors to fix GPS, heart rate and steps.
  • Health data, Segments, Goals, Training plans, the Heat map and the Gallery.
  • Compare: up to ten activities side by side, including a virtual race and the passes of a segment.
  • Settings and User settings.

How the figures are computed is explained under Metrics, starting with how a file becomes an activity.

docs.title: Building it yourself
docs.text:
You need Rust, Node.js 22 with pnpm, and the Tauri prerequisites for your system.

cd app
pnpm install
pnpm tauri dev     # run in development mode
pnpm tauri build   # build the installer

docs.title: Activity data
docs.text: This page explains how a file you import becomes an activity: which values RunningMate reads from the file, which it computes, and with which formulas. Everything here happens once on import and again whenever an activity is recomputed (after a route fix, a reset to the original, or one of the data fixes described at the end).

docs.title: Reading the file
docs.text:
RunningMate reads TCX and GPX files.

  • TCX: every <Trackpoint> with a time is read, with its position, altitude, heart rate, cadence (RunCadence) and power (Watts). Calculations only use trackpoints that have a position and an altitude. Points without them stay in the file, for example as anchors for the route fix editor.
  • GPX (1.0 and 1.1, e.g. from Garmin, Strava or Komoot): every <trkpt> with a time is read from all tracks. A point without <ele> takes the altitude of the point before it (0 m before the first). Heart rate and cadence come from Garmin's track point extension (hr, cad), power from a power element. The GPX is converted to TCX and archived as TCX, with the original GPX kept next to it. A GPX without times is a planned route, not a recording, and is rejected.

The sport comes from the TCX Sport attribute, or from the GPX <type>, which apps fill freely: anything containing "run", "jog" or "lauf" becomes a run ("trail" a trail run), "cycl", "bik", "ride", "rad" or "velo" a ride, "walk", "hik", "wander" or "trek" a walk. Strava's old numbers work too (1 ride, 9 run, 10 walk, 11 hike). A GPX without a type counts as a run. A TCX with the sport "Other" counts as a walk.

A file that has times but no GPS at all (a treadmill run, a watch with GPS switched off) isn't imported straight away. It waits until you draw its route in the route fix editor.

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text: A file is skipped if a file with the same name (without .tcx or .gpx) was imported before, so a run exported in both formats is only imported once. It is also skipped if an activity on the same day has about the same distance: within 1 %, and at least within 50 m. That catches the same run recorded by two devices or apps.

docs.title: Clock jumps
docs.text: Some devices write wrong times, for example a run whose first trackpoints are dated correctly and all later ones two weeks too late. A gap of more than 12 hours between two trackpoints is treated as such a clock jump, not a pause: every time after it moves back so that it follows the point before by one second, keeping the spacing of the times after it. The activity then starts on the right day.

docs.title: Duration and pauses
docs.text:
The duration is the elapsed time from the first to the last trackpoint, pauses included.

A pause is any gap of more than 10 seconds between two consecutive trackpoints. Devices with auto-pause stop writing trackpoints while you stand still, which leaves such gaps. The activity's pause time is the sum of all of them. Standing still while the device keeps recording every second is not a pause.

Moving time is the duration minus the pause time. It isn't shown on the activity itself, but the cardio fitness estimate (see Fitness and form) and the training plan use it.

docs.title: Distance
docs.text: The distance adds up the straight lines between consecutive trackpoints. For the activity's total the positions are first projected onto a flat map (UTM, in the zone of the track's mean longitude); the splits and the per-point speed use the distance on the earth's ellipsoid (WGS84) instead. Over an activity both agree to within a few metres.

docs.title: Elevation gain
docs.text: The elevation gain is the sum of all rises between consecutive trackpoints, in metres. Descents don't subtract anything. The altitudes are used as recorded, without smoothing, so a noisy barometer or GPS altitude adds a little gain.

docs.title: Speed and pace per point
docs.text:
For every trackpoint RunningMate computes a speed and a pace from the distance and time to the point before:

  • When more than 80 % of the gaps between trackpoints are exactly one second, the time gaps are smoothed over five points first, so speed and pace don't jump with every GPS fix. Pauses, steps and calories always use the real gaps.
  • Where you stood still (no distance between two points), the distance is filled in from the neighbouring points, so a stop doesn't produce an extreme pace.
  • A pace outside the range a person can manage for the activity type is left out:
Activity Pace kept Minimum step Run 3:00–12:00 min/km 0.5 m Ride 0:30–6:00 min/km (10–120 km/h) 5 m Walk 8:00–25:00 min/km 0.2 m

Steps shorter than the minimum get no pace. How these values add up to the averages you see is described under Pace.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
If the file has power (a power meter or a running power pod), the measured watts are used. Otherwise RunningMate estimates them from the speed (m/s) and the climb rate (metres climbed per second) of each point, using your body weight from the user settings (70 kg if none is set).

Runs and walks use the energy above resting from the ACSM metabolic equations (see Calories below), a quarter of which becomes mechanical power:

with , for running and , for walking. That gives roughly 1 W per kg per m/s, which is what running power meters show. A 68 kg runner at 2.36 m/s (6:47 min/km) on the flat comes out at about 168 W.

Rides use rolling resistance and air drag, with an 8 kg bike, a rolling resistance coefficient of 0.004, air density 1.225 kg/m³ and a drag area of 0.27 m²:

The ride estimate has no climbing term, so it underestimates the power on a climb. The average power of the activity is the mean of the per-point values.

docs.title: Calories
docs.text:
Runs and walks use the ACSM metabolic equations (American College of Sports Medicine). They give the oxygen you use, in ml per kg per minute, from the speed and the grade:

with the same and as above (speed in metres per minute). Summed over the trackpoints, the speed term becomes the distance covered and the grade term the metres climbed. Downhill counts as flat. Per point:

using 5 kcal per litre of oxygen. Standing still only adds the resting term, and measured watts don't change what a run costs.

Example: 68 kg, 1 km on the flat in 6 minutes: kcal.

Rides use the power (measured or estimated), assuming 25 % of the energy you burn reaches the pedals:

A gap of more than 10 seconds (a pause) adds nothing. At a steady 150 W, an hour comes to about 516 kcal.

docs.title: Heart rate
docs.text: The average heart rate is the mean over all trackpoints that have one. Time in heart-rate zones is described under Heart rate zones.

docs.title: Steps and cadence
docs.text:
For runs and walks, TCX cadence counts one foot, so RunningMate doubles it to steps per minute.

  • Cadence (spm) is the mean of the doubled cadence over the trackpoints that have one.
  • Steps adds up cadence × 2 × the time to the previous point. Gaps of more than 10 seconds (pauses) are left out, so a pause isn't walked through at the cadence of the point after it.

Rides have no steps.

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
The activity is cut into splits of 1 km (runs and walks) or 5 km (rides). A split ends at the first trackpoint where its own distance reaches the length, so a full split is never shorter than 1 km or 5 km (it can be a few metres longer). The next split starts at that trackpoint. Whatever is left at the end becomes a shorter last split.

For each split RunningMate stores:

  • the time, from its first to its last trackpoint, pauses included;
  • the pace: that time divided by the split's distance;
  • the speed, heart rate, power and cadence as the mean of the split's trackpoints;
  • the elevation gain, the sum of the rises within the split;
  • the position of its first trackpoint.

Splits are also the basis of the fitness curve, and of the training effect and the time in zones without a track file.

docs.title: Best segments
docs.text:
For every activity RunningMate looks for the fastest stretch over fixed distances:

Activity Distances (km) Run 1, 5, 10, 21, 42 Walk 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50 Ride 5, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200

A stretch is a run of consecutive splits, starting at any split and ending as soon as the splits cover the distance. Its pace is the splits' total time over their total distance, so a short last split counts by its length. Because stretches are made of whole splits, the best 1 km of a run is its fastest 1 km split, not the fastest kilometre anywhere on the track. A stretch can't run over a split without time (a clock that ran backwards).

Records nobody can run are left out of the lists: a best segment faster than the fastest plausible pace of its activity type (3:00 min/km for runs, 0:30 min/km for rides, 8:00 min/km for walks) isn't shown. That keeps out, for example, a ride accidentally recorded as a run.

docs.title: Weather
docs.text: After the import, RunningMate looks up the weather of the day at the start of the middle split from Open-Meteo: the day's maximum and minimum temperature, precipitation, maximum wind speed and the weather code (sun, clouds, rain …). These are daily values, not the weather at the hour of the activity. Dates within the last 60 days use Open-Meteo's forecast service (which covers recent days), older dates its historical archive. The lookup is tried three times; if it still fails, or the day has no data yet, the activity has no weather.

docs.title: Data fixes at startup
docs.text:
Some values were computed wrongly by earlier versions. On startup RunningMate corrects stored activities once per database, recomputing them from their archived files:

  1. Clock jumps: activities whose file has a clock jump are imported again, so they move to the right day. A title generated from the wrong start is generated again, the AI summary is deleted and the weather is looked up again. Activities you have edited are left alone.
  2. Calories and power are recomputed with the ACSM estimates described above.
  3. Pauses and splits: calories, total steps, the splits and the best segments are recomputed with the pause handling and split cuts described above.
  4. Best segments are recomputed so that none spans a split whose clock ran backwards.
  5. Grade-adjusted pace is computed for runs and walks imported before it existed: the activity's GAP and the GAP of each split (see Pace).

Fixes 2 to 5 only change the values named; your title, comment, distance, duration and other edits stay as they are. Activities whose archived file is missing are skipped.

docs.title: Fitness and form
docs.text: The Health page and the Effect tab of the detail view show how your training adds up over weeks: fitness, fatigue and form from a training-load model, and a cardio fitness estimate (VO2max) from your runs.

docs.title: Fitness, fatigue and form
docs.text:
RunningMate uses a training-load model in the style of Banister's fitness-fatigue model, as TrainingPeaks and intervals.icu show it (CTL, ATL and TSB):

  • Fitness is a slow average of your training load, over about 42 training days.
  • Fatigue is a fast average, over about 7 training days.
  • Form is fitness minus fatigue. After hard weeks fatigue is above fitness and form is negative; after easy days it turns positive.

docs.title: Load of an activity
docs.text:
Every split with a heart rate and a pace has a load

with the average heart rate (bpm), the pace (min/km) and the speed (m/s) of the split, also for rides. (The training effect uses its own model, based on EPOC.) An activity's load is the mean of its splits' loads, weighted by the activity type:

Activity Weight Run 1.0 Ride 0.8 Walk 0.5

The loads of all activities on the same day (by UTC date) are added up to the day's load. Splits without heart rate have no load, and an activity recorded without heart rate isn't a training day at all, so it doesn't pull the curve down.

docs.title: The curve
docs.text:
The curve starts at your first activity with heart rate, with fitness and fatigue both set to that day's load. On each later training day, with that day's load :

Unlike TrainingPeaks, the averages only move on days with training: a rest day doesn't lower fitness or fatigue, the next activity does. Form includes the day's own training.

The curve is always computed from your first activity on, also when the chart only shows a part of it, so a day has the same values in every period you look at.

Example: fitness and fatigue both stand at 100. Your next training day has a load of 200:

  • fitness:
  • fatigue:
  • form:

docs.title: On the Effect tab
docs.text: The detail view shows fitness, fatigue and form for the 90 days up to the activity, as raw values.

docs.title: On the Health page
docs.text:
The load numbers have no unit anyone knows, so the Health page shows them as shares:

  • Fitness is your fitness on the last training day of the period as a share of the highest fitness you ever reached up to the end of the period, your personal best. Below it is the change over the period, from the first to the last training day in it: %.
  • Form is form as a share of fitness, %, rated in Joe Friel's zones as intervals.icu shows them:
Form Zone Meaning below −30 % High risk Fatigue is far above your fitness; too much of this risks overtraining. −30 to −10 % Optimal A productive training load: your fitness is building. −10 to +5 % Grey zone Maintaining: not much building, not much recovering. +5 to +20 % Fresh Rested and fit: a good time for a race or a test. above +20 % Transition Very rested: without training your fitness starts to drop.

A value on a boundary belongs to the zone above it (−10 % is the grey zone). In the example above, form is % of fitness: Optimal.

docs.title: Cardio fitness (VO2max)
docs.text:
VO2max is the most oxygen your body can use, in ml per kg of body weight per minute. RunningMate has no lab or watch measurement, so it estimates it from your runs with Jack Daniels' and Jimmy Gilbert's VDOT formula: the oxygen cost of the pace you ran, divided by the share of VO2max you can hold for that long.

For a run of metres in minutes of moving time (duration minus pauses), with the velocity in metres per minute:

  • Only runs of at least 3 km in the chosen period count.
  • Results below 15 or above 85 are treated as recording errors and dropped.
  • At least 3 runs are needed. Training runs aren't all-out races, so the estimate is the 90th percentile of the runs' values: it reflects your harder runs without trusting a single outlier (for example a run with a wrongly recorded pause).
  • With fewer runs, the VO2max from your user settings is shown instead, if you entered one.

Example: 5 km in 25:00 gives m/min, a cost of about 36.0 and a share of about 0.94, so a VO2max of about 38.3.

docs.title: Rating
docs.text:
With your birthday and sex in the user settings, the estimate is compared with people of the same sex and age group (20–29, 30–39 … 70–79; younger or older ages use the nearest group), using the Cooper Institute norms that Garmin uses. The age is your age at the end of the period. The levels start at these values (ml/kg/min):

Age Men: Fair Good Excellent Superior Women: Fair Good Excellent Superior 20–29 41.7 45.4 51.1 55.4 36.1 39.5 43.9 49.6 30–39 40.5 44.0 48.3 54.0 34.4 37.8 42.4 47.4 40–49 38.5 42.4 46.4 52.5 33.0 36.3 39.7 45.3 50–59 35.6 39.2 43.4 48.9 30.1 33.0 36.7 41.1 60–69 32.3 35.5 39.5 45.7 27.5 30.0 33.0 37.8 70–79 29.4 32.3 36.7 42.1 25.9 28.1 30.9 36.7

Below the Fair value the level is Poor. In the example, 38.3 is Good for a woman of 45 and Fair for a man of 55.

docs.title: Heart rate zones
docs.text: Heart rate zones sort the intensity of your training by heart rate, from easy recovery to all-out efforts. RunningMate uses five zones. In the user settings you choose how they are set: you enter them yourself, or they are worked out from your maximum heart rate or from your heart-rate reserve. Until zones are set, the detail view and the Health page show no time in zones.

docs.title: The zones
docs.text:
Each zone is given by its upper bound in beats per minute. Each zone starts one beat above the previous one.

Zone From To Zone 1 the start of zone 1 (see the methods) zone 1 bound Zone 2 zone 1 bound + 1 zone 2 bound Zone 3 zone 2 bound + 1 zone 3 bound Zone 4 zone 3 bound + 1 zone 4 bound Zone 5 zone 4 bound + 1 zone 5 bound

A heart rate counts in the first zone whose upper bound it doesn't exceed. A heart rate below the start of zone 1 still counts as zone 1, one above the zone 5 bound still counts as zone 5.

All analyses use the same zones: the time in zones, the colours of the heart-rate chart, the reference lines, the check of easy runs in a training plan and the facts for the AI summary.

docs.title: Custom
docs.text:
You enter the five upper bounds yourself, for example from a lab test or your watch. Each bound must be a whole number between 40 and 240 bpm and higher than the one before. Zone 1 starts at half of the zone 5 bound.

Before you save bounds, the form suggests some at 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 % of your maximum heart rate, rounded down:

  • the maximum heart rate from your profile, if you have entered one;
  • otherwise the age-predicted maximum , with your age taken from your birthday.

Example: with a maximum heart rate of 185 bpm the suggestion is 111, 129, 148, 166 and 185 bpm. Zone 1 then runs from 92 (half of 185, rounded down) to 111 bpm, zone 2 from 112 to 129 bpm, and so on. Without a maximum heart rate, at 56 years the formula gives bpm and the bounds 98, 114, 131, 147 and 164.

Custom bounds stay as they are when you change your profile.

docs.title: Percent of maximum heart rate
docs.text:
The zones end at 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 % of the maximum heart rate from your profile, and zone 1 starts at 50 %. Each bound is , rounded down, with = 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9 and 1.0 (0.5 for the start of zone 1). These are the bounds of the suggestion above, but they follow your profile: a new maximum heart rate moves the zones with it. The age formula isn't used here; the method needs a maximum heart rate in the profile.

Example: at 185 bpm the zones end at 111, 129, 148, 166 and 185 bpm and zone 1 starts at 92 bpm.

docs.title: Karvonen (heart-rate reserve)
docs.text:
The Karvonen method takes the same shares of your heart-rate reserve, the range between resting and maximum heart rate, and adds them to the resting heart rate. Each bound is , rounded down, with the same as above. Since the resting heart rate is part of it, the zones sit higher than with a plain percentage of the maximum, most of all in the lower zones. The method needs both heart rates in the profile, and the resting one must be below the maximum.

Example: with a resting heart rate of 50 and a maximum of 185 bpm the reserve is 135 bpm. Zone 1 starts at bpm and the zones end at 131, 144, 158, 171 and 185 bpm.

docs.title: Time in zones of an activity
docs.text:
The Zones tab of the detail view (and the heart-rate chart on the Effect tab for runs and rides) uses every trackpoint of the activity's archived file. Each trackpoint's heart rate counts for the time since the trackpoint before it:

  • gaps of more than 30 seconds are left out, so a pause isn't counted at the heart rate you had when you started again;
  • trackpoints without a heart rate (or with 0) are left out.

The percentages are shares of the time with a heart rate, not of the whole duration.

Example: your watch records every second, and a trackpoint at 142 bpm follows one a second earlier. With the bounds above (zone 3 up to 148), that second counts in zone 3.

docs.title: Without the track file
docs.text: If the archived file of an activity is missing, RunningMate falls back to the splits: each split counts its full time at its average heart rate. That is coarser: a kilometre that averaged 150 bpm counts entirely in one zone, even if you spent half of it lower and half higher.

docs.title: On the Health page
docs.text: The time in zones on the Health page always uses the splits method, over all activities of any type in the chosen period. It is therefore a little coarser than the per-activity view.

docs.title: Reference lines
docs.text: The heart-rate trend charts (detail view and Health page) draw your zone 1, zone 3 and zone 5 bounds as the Min, Ideal and Max lines. The trend line is the mean of your last 30 activities' average heart rates (on the detail view only activities of the same type in the 90 days up to the activity).

docs.title: Pace
docs.text:
Pace is the time you need per kilometre (min/km), speed the distance per hour (km/h). RunningMate shows several of both, and they aren't all computed the same way. This page explains which is which, so you know why, for example, the average pace and the average speed of an activity don't always match.

All paces are the actual paces on the terrain you covered. For runs and walks RunningMate also computes a grade-adjusted pace (GAP) as a separate value: the pace the same effort would have given on the flat. It never replaces the pace; hills also show up in the calories and power, which count the metres you climbed.

docs.title: Elapsed time and pauses
docs.text:
The duration of an activity is the elapsed time from the first to the last trackpoint, pauses included. A pause is any gap of more than 10 seconds between two trackpoints, which is what devices with auto-pause leave when you stop. The Pause value on the detail view is the sum of those gaps. Waiting at a traffic light with the device still recording every second is not a pause.

Moving time (duration minus pauses) is used for the cardio fitness estimate and the training plan, but not shown for the activity itself.

docs.title: Pace per point
docs.text:
Every trackpoint gets a pace from the distance and the time to the point before it. Points with a pace outside the plausible range for the activity type are left out: 3:00–12:00 min/km for runs, 0:30–6:00 min/km for rides and 8:00–25:00 min/km for walks. Where you stood still, the distance is filled in from the neighbouring points, and with one-second recording the time gaps are smoothed over five points. The details are under Activity data.

The pace chart on the Statistics tab shows these per-point values.

docs.title: Values of an activity
docs.text:
Value How it is computed Pauses Average speed (km/h) distance ÷ duration included Average pace (min/km) mean of the per-point paces mostly left out Fastest pace the 5th percentile of the per-point paces left out Slowest pace the 95th percentile of the per-point paces left out GAP (min/km, runs and walks) average pace × distance ÷ flat distance costing as much left out

Average speed is the plain distance over the elapsed time, so every pause and stop lowers it.

Average pace is the mean of the per-point paces. A pause is a single long gap between two points; it usually gives one implausible pace that is dropped, or one value among hundreds. Standing still while recording gets the pace of the neighbouring points. So the average pace is close to your pace while moving, and on an activity with stops it is faster than the average speed suggests.

Example: you run 10 km in 55 minutes and wait 5 minutes at traffic lights with auto-pause. The duration is 1:00:00, so the average speed is 10.0 km/h, which is a pace of 6:00 min/km. The average pace is about 5:30 min/km, your pace while moving.

The fastest and slowest pace are percentiles rather than the extremes, so a single GPS glitch doesn't set them: 5 % of your points were faster than the fastest pace, 5 % slower than the slowest.

For rides the same values are computed; the activity list shows the average pace for rides too.

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
Each split (1 km for runs and walks, 5 km for rides) has:

  • a time: from its first to its last trackpoint, pauses included;
  • a pace: that time divided by the split's distance, so a pause within the split makes it slower;
  • a speed: the mean of the split's per-point speeds, which, like the average pace, hardly notices pauses;
  • for runs and walks a GAP: the split's time over the flat distance that costs as much as the split (see below).

That is why a split's pace and speed don't always convert into each other exactly. See Activity data for how the splits are cut.

docs.title: Grade-adjusted pace (GAP)
docs.text: Running uphill costs more energy per metre than running on the flat, running gently downhill less, and running steeply downhill more again, because you brake. The grade-adjusted pace is your pace converted to the flat pace that would have cost the same energy per minute. It is computed for runs and walks, not for rides, and shown beside the pace: in the activity panel, as a column on the Splits page and as a dashed line on the pace and speed charts.

docs.title: Energy cost of a gradient
docs.text:
RunningMate uses the energy cost of running and walking on gradients measured by Minetti et al. (2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes, Journal of Applied Physiology 93: 1039–1046), in J per kg and metre for the gradient as a fraction (0.05 = 5 % uphill, −0.05 = 5 % downhill). For runs:

and for walks, from the same paper:

On the flat a run costs J/kg/m. The grade-adjusted speed is the speed times the cost on the gradient over the cost on the flat, so the grade-adjusted pace is the pace divided by it:

The cost is lowest at about −18 % for runs (−15 % for walks): there the same effort carries you fastest, so the GAP is much slower than your pace. Steeper downhill the cost rises again, and from about −40 % (−32 % for walks) the GAP is faster than your pace. Gradients steeper than ±45 %, the range Minetti measured, count as ±45 %.

docs.title: Gradient of a point
docs.text: The elevation of GPS and even barometric recordings is too noisy to take a gradient from one point to the next: a 2 m jump over 15 m is already a 13 % gradient. So the gradient of a point is the slope of a straight line fitted (least squares) to the elevation over 100 m of track around it, 50 m before and 50 m after, measured along the track. Standing still doesn't change it, and a track shorter than 20 m counts as flat. Each point's grade-adjusted pace, the dashed line on the charts, is its pace divided by the cost factor of its gradient. The point after a pause (a gap of more than 10 seconds) gets none, and neither do points without a plausible pace.

docs.title: Average GAP of an activity
docs.text:
The GAP of an activity starts from its average pace, so it treats pauses and stops the same way, and adjusts it by the energy of the whole activity:

with the average pace and the sums over the steps between the trackpoints that have a grade-adjusted pace. The second sum is the flat distance that would have cost as much as the activity. On a flat activity the GAP is the average pace. On a hilly loop it is faster: a climb costs more than the same descent saves (5 % up costs 1.301 times the flat, 5 % down 0.763 times, together more than twice the flat). A plain mean of the per-point grade-adjusted paces would come out slower instead, because a pace divided by 1.301 gains less than one divided by 0.763 loses, and it wouldn't match the splits.

docs.title: GAP of a split
docs.text:
A split's GAP is formed like its pace, the split's time over a distance: the flat distance that would have cost the same energy, the sum of each step's distance times the cost factor of its gradient (a step over a pause counts as flat). So a flat split's GAP is its pace, and a pause within the split makes it slower, as it does the pace.

Example: you run a kilometre at 6:00 min/km up a steady 5 % gradient. The cost is J/kg/m, 1.301 times the 3.6 of the flat, so the GAP is min/km: the effort of running 4:37 min/km on the flat. Down the same gradient the cost is 2.746 J/kg/m (0.763 times the flat) and 6:00 min/km becomes a GAP of 7:52 min/km. Down a 45 % slope, braking costs 4.032 J/kg/m, 1.120 times the flat, and 6:00 min/km is a GAP of 5:21 min/km.

docs.title: Best segments
docs.text: The best segments are the fastest stretches of 1, 5, 10, 21 and 42 km for runs (other distances for rides and walks), made of consecutive splits. Their pace is the total time of those splits over their total distance, pauses included. Because they are built from whole splits, your best kilometre is your fastest 1 km split. Paces faster than the plausible limit of the activity type (3:00 min/km for runs) are left out as recording errors. More under Activity data.

docs.title: Trainings Effect
docs.text:
The Effect tab of the detail view rates what an activity did for your fitness in the way Garmin, Suunto and Polar watches do with the method of Firstbeat: from EPOC, the excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, the extra oxygen your body needs after exercise to return to rest. The harder and longer you train, the higher EPOC climbs; easy stretches let it fall again.

From the heart rate of the activity RunningMate works out

  • the peak EPOC in ml of oxygen per kg of body weight,
  • the aerobic training effect from 0.0 to 5.0, from the peak EPOC and your fitness level,
  • the anaerobic training effect from 0.0 to 5.0, from the time close to your maximum heart rate,
  • the recovery time in hours.

Firstbeat's model is proprietary. Its published form (the white paper EPOC Based Training Effect Assessment) is followed here, but the formulas and constants below are RunningMate's own approximation: the values come close to what a watch shows, but they won't be the same.

Beside it, the Effect tab shows the effect score from 1 to 12, RunningMate's own rating carried over from the first version of the app. It compares the activity with your training of the last 90 days instead.

docs.title: Data used
docs.text:
• The heart rate of every trackpoint of the archived activity file. Each point's heart rate counts for the time since the previous point. Without a recorded track, the splits are used instead: each split's average heart rate for its duration. Without any heart rate there is no training effect.
  • Your maximum and resting heart rate from the user settings. When one is missing, a fallback is used (see Fallbacks); the Effect tab says which.
  • Your VO2max for the fitness level: estimated from your runs of the 90 days up to the activity, as on the Health page, or the value from your profile when there are not enough runs.

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text:
The intensity is the share of the heart-rate reserve, the range between resting and maximum heart rate (as in the Karvonen zones):

kept between 0 and 1. The share of the heart-rate reserve is close to the share of the oxygen uptake reserve, which is why Firstbeat and others use it to measure the intensity from the heart rate.

docs.title: EPOC
docs.text:
EPOC is accumulated step by step: . At a constant intensity it moves exponentially towards a steady state that depends on the intensity: upwards when the intensity is higher than what the current EPOC corresponds to, downwards (recovery) when it is lower.

  • EPOC is generated at a rate that rises exponentially with the intensity (ml/kg/min):

  • It approaches the steady state with a time constant that is short at rest and long when hard (minutes):

  • The steady state is , and after minutes at intensity

EPOC starts at 0. The peak EPOC is the highest value during the activity. Because the time constant grows with the intensity, EPOC keeps climbing during long hard efforts, while easy running levels off early: an hour at 65 % of the reserve ends at about 22 ml/kg, 45 minutes at 82 % at about 81 ml/kg.

Pauses. As for the activity data, a gap of more than 10 seconds between two trackpoints is a pause. A pause, and any stretch without heart rate, counts as rest (): EPOC only decays during it, so a pause never adds EPOC, whatever the heart rate after it.

docs.title: Aerobic training effect
docs.text:
The peak EPOC is compared with thresholds that grow with your fitness: a fitter athlete needs more EPOC for the same effect. For an average VO2max of 45 ml/kg/min they are

Aerobic effect 1 2 3 4 5 Peak EPOC (ml/kg) 6 15 35 80 180

For your VO2max they are multiplied by the fitness factor

kept between 0.75 and 1.4; without a VO2max . Up to the first threshold the effect rises linearly from 0 to 1; between two thresholds and it is interpolated on a log scale:

and from the last threshold on it is 5.0. The effect is shown with one decimal.

docs.title: Anaerobic training effect
docs.text:
Firstbeat's anaerobic training effect also looks at the speed or power of short, hard bursts. RunningMate only has the heart rate, which reacts too slowly to see a sprint, so this is a rough approximation from the time spent close to the maximum:

  1. Anaerobic load. Every minute above 85 % of the reserve counts, weighted by the square of how far above:

    (minutes)

  2. Repeated bursts. A burst is a stretch of at least 15 seconds at 90 % of the reserve or more (zone 5 of the Karvonen zones). Every burst after the first raises the load by 25 %, up to +200 %, so intervals count more than the same time in one piece:

  3. Effect. , shown with one decimal.

An activity that never gets above 85 % of the reserve has an anaerobic effect of 0.0.

docs.title: The scale
docs.text:
Both effects use the usual wording:

Effect Meaning 0.0–0.9 No effect 1.0–1.9 Minor 2.0–2.9 Maintaining 3.0–3.9 Improving 4.0–4.9 Highly improving 5.0 Overreaching

docs.title: Recovery time
docs.text:
The recovery time grows with the peak EPOC relative to the threshold of aerobic effect 3:

at most 96 hours. An activity at the threshold of effect 3 needs a day. Above 24 hours it is shown in whole days.

docs.title: Fallbacks
docs.text:
Missing Used instead Maximum heart rate the upper bound of zone 5; else from your birthday on the day of the activity; else 185 bpm Resting heart rate 60 bpm (also when the entered value is less than 20 bpm below the maximum) VO2max an average fitness level, Track the split averages

A maximum heart rate set too low makes every activity look harder, a resting heart rate set too high as well. The Effect tab lists the heart rates and the VO2max it used and where they come from.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
You run 50 minutes at a steady 150 bpm. Your profile has a resting heart rate of 55 and a maximum of 185, and your runs give a VO2max of 50.

  • Intensity: .
  • Generation: ml/kg/min; time constant minutes; steady state ml/kg.
  • Peak EPOC after 50 minutes: ml/kg.
  • Fitness factor : the thresholds of effect 3 and 4 are about 38.9 and 88.9 ml/kg.
  • Aerobic effect: , Improving.
  • Anaerobic effect: the heart rate stays below 85 % of the reserve, so 0.0, no effect.
  • Recovery: hours, shown as 1 day.

Some more examples for an average fitness level (VO2max 45):

Activity Peak EPOC Aerobic Anaerobic Recovery 30 min at 60 % 12 ml/kg 1.7 0.0 10 h 60 min at 65 % 22 ml/kg 2.5 0.0 17 h 120 min at 70 % 38 ml/kg 3.1 0.0 25 h 45 min at 82 % 81 ml/kg 4.0 0.0 45 h 5 × 5 min at 93 % with 3 min easy, warm-up and cool-down 101 ml/kg 4.3 3.1 53 h 45 min at 92 % 174 ml/kg 5.0 2.4 80 h

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• The training effect is based on heart rate only. A heart rate that runs high from heat, caffeine, illness or a slipping chest strap raises it; one that lags behind short sprints lowers the anaerobic effect.
  • The aerobic effect depends on your fitness level, so the same run rates lower as your VO2max rises.
  • Your heart rate zones aren't used, except for the zone 5 bound as a fallback for the maximum heart rate; they are only used for the time in zones.
  • The fitness, fatigue and form chart on the same tab is described under Fitness and form.

docs.title: The effect score (1–12)
docs.text:
The effect score is a simpler rating that doesn't need your maximum or resting heart rate. It compares how hard the activity was with how hard your activities of the same sport were in the 90 days before it, using the averages of the splits.

Load. For runs and walks the load of a split is its average heart rate times its pace (min/km) over its speed (m/s) plus one; for rides the power (W) takes the place of the pace:

Baseline. The mean load of all splits of the same sport in the 90 days before the activity, at least 10 (10 without any). Splits without heart rate, pace or speed (and, for rides, power) are left out, so a run recorded without a strap doesn't pull the baseline down.

Score. The activity's load from the averages of all its splits is weighted by how high its heart rate was and compared with the baseline :

An activity missing any of the averages scores 1. The suggested rest is hours, from about 8 hours for 1 to 5 days for 12.

Score Meaning 1–2 Recovery 3–5 Base endurance 6–7 Tempo 8–9 Threshold 10–11 VO2max 12 Anaerobic

Because the score is relative to your own recent training, the same run scores lower after a block of hard weeks than after a quiet month. Unlike the training effect, it doesn't know your heart-rate reserve or fitness, and as the load uses pace, a slow run at a high heart rate scores high.

docs.title: Compare
docs.text: The Compare page puts up to ten activities side by side in charts, of one sport or mixed.

docs.title: Choosing activities
docs.text:
Open it from the sidebar or with ⇧⌘C. Add activity opens a list of all activities, newest first, with the same search as the activity list: words from the title, comment or place name, and distances such as 10km (±5 %), >21, <5 or 5-10km. The buttons below the search show one sport only. Click a row to add it, click it again to take it out.

Each activity gets a colour, which it keeps while others are added or removed; the same colour marks it in every chart. The chips at the top show its date and title: click one to open the activity in the detail window, the cross removes it and Clear removes all. The selection is kept until you change it.

The arrow on a chip opens more ways to fill the page from that activity:

  • Add similar activities adds activities of the same sport that start within 200 m of it and are within 5 % of its distance, newest first, until there are ten. The start is the point where the place name was looked up, or else the first position of the track; activities without GPS have none.
  • Fastest passes of a segment and Latest passes of a segment list the segments the activity passes. Choosing one replaces the selection with the activity and the activities of the fastest (or most recent) other passes, one pass per activity, ten at most. The segment window has a Compare button that does the same with the fastest passes.

docs.title: Segment passes
docs.text: When the page shows the passes of a segment, its name appears above the charts, and Only the segment (on by default) limits the key figures, the charts over distance or time and the virtual race to the stretch of each activity that passes the segment, counted from the segment's start. On the segment the key figures are measured on the track, so there are no calories. Splits, training effect and heart-rate zones are always those of the whole activities. Adding an activity that doesn't pass the segment turns the page back into a plain comparison.

docs.title: What is compared
docs.text:
• Key figures: distance, duration, average pace (speed for rides), grade-adjusted pace, heart rate, elevation gain, calories and steps per minute, one bar per activity. A figure that none of the activities has is left out.
  • Over distance: pace (or speed), grade-adjusted pace, heart rate, elevation and steps per minute, one line per activity. Time switches the axis to the time since the start. Lines are averaged over short stretches so the tracks can share one axis.
  • Virtual race: how far each activity is behind (+) or ahead (−) of the fastest at every point, over the distance all of them cover. The fastest is the one first at the end of that distance; its line stays at zero. The times include pauses.
  • Splits: the pace (or speed) of each kilometre, or of each 5 km for rides. Rides and runs or walks together aren't compared here, since their splits differ.
  • Training effect: aerobic and anaerobic training effect, peak EPOC, recovery time and the effect score (see Trainings effect). Activities without a heart rate have no training effect.
  • Time in heart-rate zones: one bar per activity, split into the five zones.

Grade-adjusted pace and steps are only shown for runs and walks. As soon as a ride is among the activities, pace is shown as speed (km/h) for all of them, so they share one axis; a note above the charts says so.

Below each chart the legend shows which colour is which activity; click an entry to open it. Hover over a chart to see the values of all activities at that point.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard is the start page: your latest photos, goals and planned sessions, the last four weeks at a glance, your volume over time and a feed of your activities, with your statistics on the side. Open it from the sidebar or with ⇧⌘D.

Wherever an activity shows on the dashboard (a photo, a day in the calendar, a feed entry, a record), click it to open it in the detail window. Previous and next in the detail window walk through the feed, as far as it is loaded.

docs.title: Recent photos
docs.text: The top row shows the 24 latest photos of all activities, newest first. Scroll it sideways. The row is left out while no activity has photos.

docs.title: Moving back in time
docs.text:
Below the photos, the arrows move the dashboard four weeks back or forward, and the date field jumps to the four weeks up to a day you pick. The period shown is written beside them. Back to today returns to the current four weeks. You can't move past today.

The goals, the training sessions, the overview boxes, the training calendar, the volume chart and the feed follow the chosen day. The photos and the statistics on the side always show the present.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
A row of chips, one for each goal that is running or reached, see Goals. Each chip shows the goal's name with the sport's icon, a star once it is reached, and the progress of the current period as value / target with a bar. Below that, the days left and what is left to do, or the day it was reached, and the number of periods reached in a row. For a goal in one activity that hasn't been reached yet, the value is the Best so far.

A goal for a distance in one activity (for example 10 km, or 10 km in under 50 minutes) shows instead how often it was reached (times reached), large, and below it the Best time: the fastest of those activities, scaled to the goal's distance.

Click a chip, or the box at the end of the row (Goals, or Set a goal while you have none), to open the Goals page.

docs.title: Training week
docs.text: If a training plan has sessions in the week shown or the week after, they show in a row below the goals: the day, the kind of session, its distance or content, and once done or past, how it went. Today's session is highlighted. Click a session, or the calendar button at the start of the row, to open the Training page.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Three boxes on the left:

  • Activities in the last 4 weeks (Activities in these 4 weeks when you moved back in time): the number of activities of all sports, with their distance and time.
  • Fitness: your fitness as a share of your best so far (of your best) and how much it changed in the four weeks.
  • Form: your form as a share of your fitness, with its zone (for example Optimal or Fresh).

Click Fitness or Form to open the Health data page, which explains both.

docs.title: Training calendar
docs.text:
Beside the boxes, the Training calendar shows the current week and the three before it, Monday first. A day you trained has a circle that grows with the time trained, measured against the longest day of the four weeks; today has a slightly larger dot. Hover a circle to see the day's activities with distance and time; click it to open the day's first activity.

Days with a planned training session get a ring: dashed in the colour of the kind of session while it is ahead, and in the colour of how it went once it is done or past. Hover it to see the session; click an empty ring to open the Training page.

docs.title: Volume chart
docs.text: A bar chart of the last 12 weeks or months, stacked by sport (runs, rides and walks, each in its colour), with the total on top of each bar. Choose what to add up with Distance, Time or Elevation, and the bars with Weekly or Monthly; both choices are kept. Hover a bar to see the numbers per sport and the total. Other activity types are left out.

docs.title: Activity feed
docs.text:
Your activities of all sports, newest first, ten at a time; Show more loads the next ten. Each entry shows:

  • the sport's icon, the title, date and time and the type,
  • a star, a session mark or a trophy if the activity hit a goal, did a training session or is in the top 3 of a segment (hover them for the details),
  • the comment,
  • Distance, Pace (/km) (Speed for rides), Time and Elevation,
  • a map of the route and up to five photos; with more, the last one shows how many are left.

docs.title: Statistics on the side
docs.text:
The column on the right stays in view while you scroll. Pick the sport with the icons at the top (runs, rides or walks).

  • Last 4 weeks: activities, distance, time and elevation per week, as the average of the last four weeks.
  • Personal records: for each distance, the fastest stretch of that distance within any activity, with its time and pace (speed for rides) and the date. Click a record to open the activity.
  • This year and All time: the number of activities, distance, time and elevation.

docs.title: Detail Window
docs.text:
The detail window shows everything about one activity. Open it by double-clicking an activity in the list, with View details in the activity's ⋮ menu, with Open details in the activity panel, or by clicking an activity on the dashboard, in the gallery, on the goals or training pages or in a segment's ranking.

It opens on General. An activity you haven't reviewed yet (no edit, comment, photo or video) opens on Edit instead, so you can give it a title and a comment right away. The page you pick stays selected when you move to another activity.

The header shows the title, date and type, and the place the activity started (see place names), and these buttons:

  • Toggle navigation shows or hides the page names on the left; hidden, only their icons remain. The choice is kept.
  • Previous activity and Next activity move through the activities in the order of the list you opened the window from (only when you opened it from a list).
  • Maximize fills the app window; Restore size makes it smaller again. The choice is kept.
  • Close closes the window.

If a page has changes you haven't saved (the Edit page, split corrections or fixes on Fix data) and you leave it, move to another activity or close the window, the app asks Save your changes?: Save saves them and goes on, Discard drops them, Cancel stays.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
On the left is the same panel as beside the activity list: duration, pace (for runs and walks also the grade-adjusted pace), the route, distance and elevation, the Garmin Connect link, goals, training session and trophies, the weather and the best segments. Which boxes it shows is set per sport in the settings under Activity panel.

On the right you'll find:

  • Summary, a short text comparing the activity with similar and recent ones, written by a local AI model. It only shows when AI summaries are turned on in the settings under AI summary. Click Write summary (or Rewrite) to have it written; this takes a moment. The note below it names the model.
  • Photos and videos of the activity (see Photos and videos below).
  • Your comment.
  • Further figures, where available: calories, average heart rate, average power, average speed, average pace, the grade-adjusted pace (GAP, not for rides), fastest and slowest pace, cadence and steps (not for rides), pause time, and the shoes or bike.

docs.title: Photos and videos
docs.text:
Add photos and videos with the buttons above the gallery:

  • From this activity… (macOS) opens Photos from this activity: the photos and videos in your Photos library taken during the activity (from 10 minutes before the start to 10 minutes after the end). Tick the ones you want, or use Select all, and click Add. Items already added are marked. The first time, the app asks for access to your Photos library (Allow access…); nothing in it is changed or uploaded. If access was denied, Open System Settings takes you to the place to allow it.
  • From Photos… (macOS) opens the system photo picker, to pick any photo or video.
  • From files… picks files from disk (PNG, JPG, HEIC, MP4, MOV, AVI). You can also drop files from Finder onto the gallery.

Photos from the Photos library are always copied. For files from disk the app asks whether to Copy into RunningMate (the file is safe in the app's media folder) or Link to originals (saves space, but breaks if the original is moved or deleted). Tick Remember my choice to stop being asked; you can change it in the settings under General (Adding photos and videos from files). Linked files show a small link symbol; a file that can no longer be found shows File missing. Copied photos are scaled down to the photo size set under Storage in the settings; linked files are never changed.

Click a photo or video to see it in full. Move with the arrows on screen or the arrow keys, or click a thumbnail in the strip below. Slideshow shows each photo for a few seconds and plays videos to their end; the space bar starts and stops it. To remove a file, hover over it and click ×: a copied file is deleted from the media folder, for a linked one only the link is removed.

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
This page lists the splits of the activity: one per kilometre, or per 5 kilometres for rides. For each split you'll see the distance, time, pace, GAP (the grade-adjusted pace, not for rides), speed, heart rate, power, cadence (not for rides) and elevation gain, where recorded.

Click Correct heart rate and steps (only Correct heart rate for rides) to type in the average heart rate or steps per minute a split should have. On Save and recompute, the recorded values of that split are shifted so its average matches, and the activity is recomputed: the charts, zones, training effect and the other splits follow. The change is written into the stored activity file, so it also holds when the activity is processed again. Reset to original on the Fix data page undoes it.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
The map shows the track of the activity, with a light or dark map following the app's appearance. A dot marks the start and another the finish.

The buttons above the map:

  • Track, Pace and Heart rate colour the track: in one colour, or from slow to fast or low to high heart rate, with a scale beside the buttons. Pace and heart rate are only available when they were recorded.
  • Km markers (5 km markers for rides) shows or hides numbered markers at each kilometre.
  • Splits shows or hides a list of the splits beside the map, with time and speed; click one to put a position dot where it ends (the map moves there if needed, and the charts mark it).
  • Charts shows elevation, heart rate, speed and, for runs with cadence data, steps per minute over the distance below the map (hidden at first). For runs and walks the speed chart has the grade-adjusted speed as a second, dashed line. Moving the mouse over them moves the position dot along the track.

The app remembers which of these you turned on.

docs.title: Segments
docs.text:
Lists the segments this activity passes, each with its distance, grade and climb, the time, pace (speed for rides) and its place among all tries, e.g. "2 of 7". A gold, silver or bronze trophy marks the three fastest places. Click a segment to highlight it on the map, or click Open segment to see its full ranking, where this activity's passes are marked.

Arrows along the track show the direction you went, and the numbered markers the kilometres (5 km for rides), so you can tell whether a stretch went up or down. Click New segment to mark one: click on the track where it starts, then where it ends. Where the track passes the same spot more than once, the start is the first pass and the end the next pass after the start. Use the slider to fine-tune both ends, check distance, average grade, elevation gain and the elevation profile, give it a title and click Save segment. A segment must be at least 100 m long. Stop marking or Cancel leaves without saving. The app then looks for passes over the new segment in all your activities of the same sport, in the background.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: Charts over the distance of the activity: Elevation, Heart rate, Pace (faster at the top), for runs and walks Grade-adjusted pace (GAP) (the pace on the flat for the same effort, with the pace faint behind it, so you see where climbs and descents made you slower or faster) and, for runs, Steps per minute. A chart only shows when its values were recorded. Hover over a chart to read the value at a point. See Pace and Activity data for how the values are worked out.

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
• Training effect shows the aerobic and the anaerobic training effect of the activity, each from 0.0 to 5.0 on a scale of five steps with its meaning (from "No effect" to "Overreaching"), the peak EPOC in ml/kg and the recovery time. Below, it lists the maximum and resting heart rate and the VO2max it was rated with and where they come from, e.g. "estimated as 220 − age" when your profile has no maximum heart rate. Activities without heart rate have no training effect. See Trainings Effect for how it is calculated.
  • Effect score, beside it, rates the activity from 1 to 12 on twelve rising bars, compared with your training of the same sport in the last 90 days, with its meaning (from "Recovery" to "Anaerobic") and the suggested rest. See the effect score.
  • Heart rate by zone (runs and rides with heart-rate data) shows the heart rate over the time of the activity, the line coloured by your heart-rate zones over light bands for each zone. The zones are set in the user settings.
  • Fitness trend (90 days) shows fitness, fatigue and form over the 90 days up to the activity. See Fitness.

docs.title: Heart rate zones
docs.text:
Time in heart-rate zones shows, for each zone with its heart-rate range, the share and the time you spent in it during the activity. You set the zones in the user settings; without them this box asks you to. See Heart rate zones for how they work.

Heart-rate trend (90 days, same activity type) plots the average heart rate of each activity of the same type over the 90 days up to this one, with a trend line, and dashed lines at the upper bounds of zones 1, 3 and 5 (Min, Ideal, Max).

docs.title: Social share
docs.text:
Builds an image of the activity for social media. Pick a size: presets for an Instagram post (1:1) or portrait (4:5), a story (9:16), an X post (16:9) and a Facebook post, or any size of your own. Then pick a background: a gradient, a single colour, one of the activity's photos (or any image file), a light or dark map, or transparent. Photos and the map can be darkened so the text stays readable. Choose which facts to show (title, date, distance, duration, pace or speed, elevation, heart rate, calories) and the colours and sizes of the route and the text.

Each fact is its own element: the route, the title, the date and every figure can be placed anywhere. Click an element to select it, Shift-click to add more; drag to move the selection, or nudge it with the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). On a map, the map moves with the route, so it stays on its streets. The bar above the preview lines up the selection: one element (or group) on the image's left edge, centre or right edge, top, middle or bottom; several on each other. Equal space spreads three or more evenly between the outer two, or one or two evenly across the image. Group keeps elements together: clicking one selects the whole group, and it moves, lines up and spreads as one. Turn on Grid to see a grid over the preview (not in the image): dragged elements put their nearest edge or centre on its lines; hold Option (⌥) while dragging to place them freely. Reset positions puts everything back.

Save image… writes a PNG; Share… opens the macOS share menu (Messages, Mail, AirDrop, Photos and any app that offers itself there). To post on Instagram, save the image and upload it from your phone or the website. The editor remembers your last settings for the next activity.

docs.title: Edit
docs.text:
Change the Title, the Comment, the Type (e.g. Trail, Interval or Long Run for runs, Hiking for walks, Gravel Biking for rides), the Start time, the Duration (h:mm:ss), the Distance (km) and the Elevation (m), and click Save. The window then goes back to General. Changing distance, duration or elevation here doesn't change the recorded track, so the splits, charts and segment times stay as they were; to correct the track itself, use Fix data.

Beside the form, pick the Shoes (or Bike for rides) you used, or None. This applies right away and moves the distance from one item to the other. Retired items are only listed while they are assigned to this activity.

Below the form you can add and remove photos and videos, as on the General page; these changes apply right away.

To process an activity again from its file or to delete it, use Re-import from TCX or Delete… in the activity's ⋮ menu in the activity list.

docs.title: Fix data
docs.text: Corrects recording errors in the activity's track. Choose what to fix at the top: Route, Heart rate or Steps (not for rides). Fixes collect in the Fixes list, where you can remove them again; Recorded and After the fixes compare the distance (or the average heart rate or steps) before and after. Save and recompute writes the fixes into the stored activity file and recomputes the activity: distance, splits, charts, zones, training effect, segments and goals follow. The original file is kept, so Reset to original drops all fixes of route, heart rate and steps (and split corrections) and recomputes the activity from the file as it was imported.

docs.title: Route
docs.text:
The map shows the track; Problems found lists GPS spike (positions far off the route, faster than the sport allows) and GPS dropout (stretches without a position, or a long jump in time and place), marked red on the map.

  • Drag the track to move it: the stretch around the point you grab (about 250 m either side) follows.
  • Click a problem, or Pick a stretch on the map and click where the stretch starts and where it ends. Then click the map to draw the route of that stretch; drag the points to move them, Undo point takes the last one back. The stretch's time span and the new length are shown. Use route adds it to the fixes, Cancel drops it.

With Follow paths turned on, the drawn route follows OpenStreetMap paths between your points instead of straight lines. This sends the points you place to routing.openstreetmap.de; turn it off to keep everything on your computer. If no path can be found, straight lines are used.

An activity recorded without GPS (No GPS) starts with drawing the whole route.

docs.title: Heart rate and steps
docs.text:
A chart shows the recorded values (heart rate in bpm, or steps per minute) over the distance, with your changes on top. Problems found lists stretches that look wrong:

  • No values recorded: nothing at the start or the end, for example a chest strap that only connected after the first kilometre.
  • Dropout: values missing for 10 s or more in between (for steps only while you were moving, since steps stop when you stand still).
  • Implausible values: values far off the level both before and after them, by more than 20 bpm or 25 steps per minute compared with the median of the 30 s on either side. A change of level, such as a climb, a walk break or slowing down, isn't one; fewer steps while you also got slower aren't either. In the first minute only values that are too high count, since starting low and warming up is normal, but a foot pod or strap reading far too high at the start is caught.
  • Implausible start: a heart-rate strap reading high from the first seconds, then dropping suddenly and staying lower.

Click a problem or drag over the chart to select a stretch, also where nothing was recorded; you can fine-tune it in the From (km) and To (km) fields, and its average is shown. Then:

  • Estimate from the pace works out the values from how fast you went, which suits a longer stretch, such as a strap that only connected after the first kilometre. How your heart rate (or step rate) follows your speed is learned from the rest of the activity: a straight line through the recorded values against your speed over the minute before each point, while moving. Over the stretch the heart rate climbs towards that level with a delay of about 45 s, as it does when you start running; at the very start of the activity it begins at a low value, between 55 % and 75 % of the level the recording settles at. Finally the estimate is bent so it meets the recorded values on both sides. It needs at least two minutes of recorded values elsewhere in the activity.
  • Interpolate replaces the values with a straight line from the level before the stretch to the level after it, each the median of the 30 s beside the stretch, so a single stray value next to it doesn't set the level. A stretch at the start or end gets the level of its one side.
  • Set sets them all to the value you type in,
  • Shift moves them up or down by the value you type in.

To correct the average of whole splits instead, use Correct heart rate and steps on the Splits page.

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text: The gallery shows the photos and videos of all activities in one place, newest activity first.

docs.title: The Gallery page
docs.text: Open it from the sidebar or with ⇧⌘P. Filter by sport at the top; the number of photos and videos shown is at the top right. Grid shows everything as one grid of tiles; By activity groups them under the activity's title and date. The choice is kept. In By activity, clicking the title opens the activity in the detail window, where previous and next move to the neighbouring activities with photos. Videos show their first frame with a play symbol. Files that no longer exist (for example a linked original that was moved) are left out.

docs.title: Full view
docs.text:
Click a tile to see it in full. Move through the photos and videos with the arrows beside it, the arrow keys or the strip of thumbnails at the bottom. Slideshow moves on by itself, every few seconds for a photo and at the end of a video; the space bar starts and stops it while a photo is shown. Open activity opens the activity the photo belongs to.

Photos and videos are added to an activity on its edit page; the photos in the detail window open in the same full view.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text: A goal is a target you set yourself: a distance, a time, a climb or a number of activities. You can reach it in one activity ("a 10 km run in under 50 minutes") or as the total over a period ("100 km a month", "3 runs a week", "500 km in 60 days"), once or again and again.

docs.title: Setting a goal
docs.text:
Open the Goals page from the sidebar or with ⇧⌘O and click New goal.

  • Sport: all activities, or only runs, rides or walks.
  • Goal for: Distance (km), Time (hours, the elapsed time of the activities), Elevation (m climbed) or the number of Activities.
  • Target: the amount to reach, above zero.
  • Counted: All activities together adds them up over the period; In one activity needs a single activity to reach the target (the longest one, for a time). A number of activities is always a total.
  • Time limit: only for a distance or climb in one activity, the most it may take, as H:MM:SS, and optional. "10 km" with 0:50:00 is reached by any activity of at least 10 km that took 50 minutes or less.
  • Period: a Week (Monday to Sunday), a calendar Month or Year, a Number of days (1 to 3650, entered under Days), or No period: one stretch from the start date to the end date, or for good.
  • Repeat: the goal starts over in the next period, or after each window of days. Without it, the goal has a single period and is reached or missed once. A goal with no period can't repeat.
  • Start: the first day counted. Weeks, months and years follow the calendar, so the week, month or year holding the start date counts in full. A number of days runs from the start date. A start date in the past counts the activities you already did.
  • End: tick No end date to let the goal run for good, or pick the last day. With no period, the end date is the last day counted. With a period, the period holding the end date is the last one, and it counts in full.
  • Name: left empty, the goal is named after what it asks for, for example "100 km every month" or "10 km in under 0:50:00 in one activity".

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Each goal has one of these states:

  • Upcoming: the start date is still ahead.
  • Active: the goal is running.
  • Reached: a goal without repeat was reached.
  • Missed: a goal without repeat whose period is over without reaching it.
  • Ended: a repeating goal past its end date.

docs.title: Progress on the dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard shows a row of chips, one per goal that is upcoming, active or reached; missed and ended goals are left out. A chip shows the current period's progress against the target with a bar, and below it what is left to do and the days left, "Starts …" for an upcoming goal or "Reached …" once done. A goal in one activity shows Best so far until it is reached. From two periods reached in a row on, the chip adds the streak, for example "3 in a row".

A goal for a distance in one activity (for example 10 km, or 10 km in under 50 minutes) shows instead how often it was reached, large, and below it Best time: the fastest of those activities scaled to the goal's distance. A 12 km run in 57:36 counts as 48:00 for a 10 km goal. Before the first hit it says Not reached yet.

Click a chip to open the Goals page. Without any goal, the row has a Set a goal button.

When you move the dashboard back in time (the arrows and date field below the photos, four weeks a step), the chips show the goals as they stood on that day: later activities don't count yet.

docs.title: The Goals page
docs.text:
Each goal has a card with its state, what it asks for and its dates, the current period with its progress and days left, and the earlier periods as small bars, oldest on the left, up to twelve of them. A bar is filled in the sport's colour where the target was reached and fainter the further it was from the target; hover it for the period and its value. Below the bars:

  • Periods reached, for a repeating goal: reached periods out of those that are over or reached.
  • In a row, for a repeating goal: the streak of periods reached in a row up to now. A running period that isn't reached yet doesn't break it.
  • Activities with a star, and the latest of them; click it to open the activity.

Filter by sport at the top. You can edit, archive or delete a goal from its card. Archived goals are hidden from the dashboard and the list unless you tick Show archived, and keep their stars. Restore brings an archived goal back. Deleting a goal removes its stars; the activities stay as they are.

docs.title: Stars
docs.text:
An activity that hit a goal shows a star, on the dashboard feed and in the activity panel, with the number of goals when it hit several. Hover it to see which goals it hit.

  • For a goal in one activity, every activity that reaches it gets a star.
  • For a total, the activity that took the total past the target in its period gets the star.

Progress and stars are worked out from the activities each time, so importing, editing or deleting an activity updates them right away.

docs.title: Health Data
docs.text: The Health data page shows how your fitness, form and heart rate develop over a period, across all your activities. Open it from the sidebar or with ⇧⌘H, or click Fitness or Form on the dashboard. How the values are calculated is explained in Fitness and form.

docs.title: Period
docs.text: At the top, pick 1 month, 3 months, 6 months or 1 year (up to today), or set your own From and To dates. The page opens with the last 3 months. While a date is missing or From is after To, the page keeps showing the last valid period, dimmed.

docs.title: Key numbers
docs.text:
Four cards for the period:

  • Activities: the number of activities, and how many of them have heart-rate data.
  • Average heart rate: the mean of the activities' average heart rates.
  • Fitness: your fitness at the end of the period as a share of the highest fitness you ever reached up to then (of your best, with its date), and how much it changed during the period.
  • Form: your form at the end of the period as a share of your fitness, with its zone and date.

Fitness and form are shown as percentages because the load points behind them have no unit of their own: compare them over time, not with other apps.

docs.title: Cardio fitness (VO2max)
docs.text:
An estimate of your VO2max in ml/kg/min, from your faster runs of 3 km or more in the period; it needs at least 3 such runs. With fewer, the value from your user settings is shown, if you entered one.

With your birthday and sex in the user settings, the value is rated Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent or Superior against people of your age group and sex (Cooper Institute norms, as used by Garmin), and a coloured scale shows where you are: the darker, the fitter.

docs.title: Form
docs.text:
Your form as a share of your fitness, on a scale of five zones:

Zone Form Meaning High risk below −30 % Fatigue is far above your fitness; too much of this risks overtraining. Optimal −30 to −10 % A productive training load: your fitness is building. Grey zone −10 to 5 % Maintaining: not much building, not much recovering. Fresh 5 to 20 % Rested and fit: a good time for a race or a test. Transition above 20 % Very rested: without training your fitness starts to drop.

docs.title: Fitness, fatigue and form
docs.text: A line chart of the three values for every day of the period. Fitness is your training load averaged over about six weeks, fatigue over about one week, and form is the difference. Hover the chart to read the values of a day.

docs.title: Average heart rate per activity
docs.text: One dot per activity with heart-rate data, coloured by sport (runs, rides, walks), and a grey Trend line: the average over the last 30 activities. With heart-rate zones set, dashed lines mark Min, Ideal and Max at the upper limits of zones 1, 3 and 5.

docs.title: Time in heart-rate zones
docs.text: How much of the period's training time you spent in each heart-rate zone, as a bar with the share and the time, and the zone's heart-rate range. Set your zones in the user settings to see this.

docs.title: Heat Map
docs.text: The heat map draws the GPS track of every activity on one map. Each track is a thin, see-through line, so roads and trails you use often add up to a brighter line, and places you went to only once stay faint.

docs.title: The Heat Map page
docs.text: Open it from the sidebar or with ⇧⌘M. At first it shows all activities of all sports. Filter by sport at the top, and limit the period with From and To; Any time clears the dates again. The map zooms to the tracks of the selection and the number of activities shown is at the top right. Activities without a GPS track, such as treadmill runs, are left out.

docs.title: How the tracks are kept
docs.text: For the heat map, each track is simplified once (points that lie within about 5 m of the line are dropped) and stored with the activity. New activities get their track when they are imported. Activities imported before the heat map existed get it the first time they are shown, which can take a moment with many activities. After that, opening the page or changing the filters only reads the stored tracks. Re-importing an activity or fixing its route in the detail window stores its track again. Deleting an activity removes its track as well.

docs.title: Main Window
docs.text: The main window has a title bar at the top, the sidebar on the left and the current page beside it. On the activity pages a details panel on the right shows one activity.

docs.title: Title bar
docs.text: The title bar shows the name of the current page. The button on the left collapses the sidebar to its icons and opens it again (also ⌘B). On the activity pages, the button on the right (Toggle details panel) shows or hides the details panel; the choice is kept.

docs.title: Sidebar
docs.text:
The sidebar has three groups of pages. Hover an entry to see its shortcut; the same pages are in the View menu.

Entry Shortcut Page Dashboard ⇧⌘D The start page, see Dashboard All, Runs, Rides, Walks The activities of all sports or of one sport (below) Health data ⇧⌘H Fitness, form and heart rate, see Health data Segments ⇧⌘G See Segments Goals ⇧⌘O See Goals Training ⇧⌘T See Training Heat map ⇧⌘M See Heat map Gallery ⇧⌘P See Gallery

At the bottom:

  • Sync (⌘O) imports activities from files, a folder or Garmin Connect, see Sync.
  • Search (⌘F) opens the activities with the search bar, see Search and filters.
  • User opens your profile, shoes, bikes and heart-rate zones, see User settings.
  • Settings (⌘,) opens the app settings, see Settings.

The app opens on the dashboard.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text: All, Runs, Rides and Walks show the activities of that sport. Switching sport keeps a search or filter, but goes back to the first page and to sorting by date.

docs.title: Info cards and training calendar
docs.text:
At the top, four cards add up the activities shown: Activities, Distance, Duration and Elevation.

Below them is a calendar of the last 52 weeks, one square per day and one column per week (Monday at the top). The more time you trained that day, the stronger the colour, measured against the busiest day in the calendar. Hover a square to see the date and the training time. With a date filter, the calendar ends on the To date (or a year after the From date).

Both follow the sport and any search or filter.

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
The columns depend on the sport:

  • All: Type, Date, Title, Duration, Distance (km).
  • Runs: Date, Title, Duration, Distance (km), Elevation (m), Speed (km/h), Pace (/km), HR (bpm), Steps, Pause.
  • Rides: as runs, with Power (W) instead of Steps.
  • Walks: as runs, without Pause.

The button at the right end of the header row (Columns) adds optional columns: Location, the place the activity started in (see Settings), shown after the title. The choice is kept.

Click a column header to sort by it, and again to reverse the order; an arrow marks the sorted column. The first two columns stay in place when you scroll the table sideways. The table shows 25 activities a page; the arrows below it move between pages.

  • Click a row to show the activity in the details panel.
  • Double-click a row to open it in the detail window. Previous and next in the detail window follow the order of the table, across pages.
  • The ⋮ button at the end of a row opens a menu:
    • View details opens the detail window.
    • Re-import from TCX processes the stored activity file again, for example after an update of RunningMate changed how something is calculated.
    • Upload to Garmin Connect uploads the activity (sign in under Sync first).
    • Delete… deletes the activity, see Deleting.

docs.title: Search and filters
docs.text:
Click Search in the sidebar, choose View → Search or press ⌘F to show the search bar above the activities; the same again hides it. Type to search: the list updates after a short pause. The search ignores upper and lower case and looks in the title, the comment and the place the activity started in.
